candidate.blueprint_locator: Management of Care — Informed Consent, printed p.22 (PDF p.25)
candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed consent and decision-making capacity
candidate.educational_objective: Before relying on informed consent, verify that the client can meaningfully understand and decide; when current decision-making capacity is impaired, pause elective care and follow the appropriate provider/surrogate consent process.

options.A: Ask the client to sign immediately because the procedure is already scheduled
options.B: Do not obtain a new consent signature from the client in the current state; notify the appropriate provider and follow the consent process for a client who cannot presently demonstrate decision-making capacity
options.C: Ask any available family member to sign because family presence automatically creates legal authority to consent
options.D: Proceed without consent because administration of procedural sedation creates an emergency exception

candidate.rationale: Valid informed consent requires the ability to understand relevant information, consider alternatives, and make a voluntary decision. The stem establishes that the client is currently drowsy, confused, and unable to explain the procedure or alternatives, so the nurse should not treat a new signature obtained in that state as adequate informed consent. The appropriate provider should be notified and the applicable process for decision-making incapacity and an authorized surrogate, if needed, should be followed. A family member is not automatically a legally authorized surrogate, and routine elective care does not become an emergency merely because sedation has already been administered.
candidate.source_claim_supported: AMA identifies decision-making ability as a required element of informed consent; NCSBN defines the RN role as participating in and verifying informed consent rather than treating a signature alone as sufficient.
candidate.source_document_title: AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 2.1.1 — Informed Consent; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
candidate.source_locator: AMA Opinion 2.1.1: assess the patient's ability to understand relevant medical information, treatment alternatives, and make an independent voluntary decision. NCSBN Management of Care — Informed Consent, printed p.22 (PDF p.25): identify appropriate person, participate in consent, verify education and consent.

candidate.stem: An elective procedure is about to begin, but no informed-consent form has been signed. The client has already received IV sedation and is now drowsy, confused, and unable to explain the procedure or its alternatives. What should the nurse do?
